rows.quote: I renewed it for a year ($14.99).

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you — and sorry for the slow reply. There is something concrete, and it happens to be analyst-shaped, so let me describe it properly and you can tell me whether it appeals. The thing I keep coming back to is this. Almost every proposal for governing advanced AI — audits, incident reporting, licensing, capability thresholds — assumes that someone outside the company can check whether a commitment was kept. I don't think that assumption holds, and as far as I can tell nobody has measured it. So: collect the public safety commitments frontier AI developers have made, record each one verbatim from an archived source, and score it on whether an outsider could ever tell it had been broken. Five dimensions, 0-3 each: how specific the promised action is, how clearly the trigger is defined, whether compliance leaves any externally observable trace, whether anyone independent checks, and whether any consequence is stated. The headline number is the share of commitments that are externally falsifiable at all. My hunch — which is exactly the kind of hunch that deserves to be checked rather than asserted — is that the common failure isn't vague promises. The actions are often quite specific. It's that the trigger rests on an internal judgement: \"if our risk assessment finds...\". Specific action, discretionary trigger. Unfalsifiable from outside. What I'd want from a second person, and why it's real work rather than busywork: the scoring has to be double-coded blind to be worth anything. Two people score the same commitments independently, we measure inter-coder agreement, we publish the agreement statistics even when they're bad, and every disagreement gets adjudicated into the codebook. Without that it's one person's opinion in a spreadsheet. So the role is second coder, plus the reliability statistics and data hygiene. Roughly five hours a week, which is the cadence the project is designed around rather than a coincidence. Two things I want to be straight about before you say yes: It's unpaid right now. I'm applying for a grant that would include a stipend for exactly this role, but I don't have it, and you shouldn't count on it. If it comes through, it's yours. And the first month is deliberately unglamorous: hardening the rubric, arguing about edge cases, and coding the same fifteen commitments cold so we can see how badly we disagree. That part is annoying and it is also the part that determines whether any of the later numbers mean anything. You'd be credited by name on every release, and your view would carry real weight on the methodology — I'd rather you disagreed with me early than politely went along with a rubric that doesn't work. If that sounds like your idea of a good use of five hours, I'll send you the draft rubric and the four open questions I most want attacked. And if it doesn't, genuinely no awkwardness — tell me what you'd rather do and I'll see if it fits, or point you at someone better. Best, Morgan"
rows.quote: Priya (a real scoped role, with the unpaid status stated plainly)

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Idris Bellamy <grants@emberfallfund.org> with subject "Re: Rapid grants — yes, you can still apply". It read: "Hi Idris, Thanks for confirming, and good to meet you too. I'm intending to apply before the 30th. The proposal is drafted; I have one administrative thing to clear first (an outside-activities disclosure with my employer), and since the named applicant signs the grant agreement I'd rather have that squared away before I put my name on a form than after. So you know what's coming: the project is a public dataset measuring whether the safety commitments frontier AI developers make can be checked by anyone outside those companies. Each commitment recorded verbatim from an archived source and scored on specificity, trigger clarity, external observability, independent attestation, and stated consequence. The headline output is the share of public commitments that are externally falsifiable at all. Quarterly releases, double-coded with published inter-coder reliability, CC-BY, with a right of reply for every developer scored. Likely ask is around $12,000, almost all of it a stipend for a part-time second coder — no compensation for me. The short version of why: audits, incident reporting and licensing all assume an outsider can check something, and I don't think anyone has measured whether that's true of the commitments already on the record. One question, if you have a moment. You mention a two-page proposal and a simple budget — is there a format you prefer, and would the fund rather see a narrower pilot it can evaluate at the end of the year, or the full twelve-month programme? I'd rather ask than guess. If the disclosure drags and I'm going to miss the 30th, I'll tell you rather than go quiet. Best, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold"
rows.quote: Idris at Emberfall (holding reply plus a format question).

rows.text: Created a recurring schedule named "Halcyon Threshold weekly review" (0 8 * * 1) that starts new sessions of the agent.
